decisions.question: decide how a `reduceInto` sink maps to a write chain

options.label: One write chain per reduceInto
options.consequence: Its fold and the stages that feed its events form one chain: a reducer that throws, or an error that reaches the sink, ends it and cancels the events stages that feed no other live chain; the state topic keeps its value. Matches Spec Appendix A.1, which defines reduceInto as a scan seeded with the topic's current value, so a reduceInto is a write of a scan.

options.label: A reducer error skips the event and the fold goes on
options.consequence: Treats the reducer unlike every other transformer; contradicts Spec §10.2 principle 4 (transformers must not throw; a throw ends the chain) and v1 G26's 'a reducer that throws ends its reduceInto'.

options.label: reduceInto keeps v1's sink-only end
options.consequence: On Dart the events pipeline of an ended reduceInto keeps running, the platform-dependent stopping point Spec §10.2 principle 5 removes; the reduce-chain case cannot be written.

decisions.why: The Specification itself reads reduceInto as a write of a scan (Appendix A.1 'Reducer topology'), and the write chain is defined by the write declaration (Appendix A.4), so the reduceInto's events pipeline plus its fold is the chain. v1 already ended a reduceInto on a reducer throw; v2 extends that to cancelling what feeds it. This timestamp is an upper bound reconstructed from file birth times, because date -u was not run at the moment of the decision (see notes_for_orchestrator).

decisions.question: When does an error end a write chain: the first error raised anywhere in its pipeline (Spec §10.2 principle 5's 'The first error in a write chain ends that chain', read literally) or the first error that reaches its sink unrecovered?

options.label: The first error that reaches the sink unrecovered
options.consequence: A catchError on the error's path keeps the chain alive; v1's 'reaches a sink' criterion stays; matches principle 2 (authors apply catchError to prevent termination; a chain terminates 'due to an unhandled exception') and the intake's L3 'first unhandled error'.

options.label: Any error raised in the chain
options.consequence: catchError could never keep a chain alive, contradicting principle 2 and Guide §4's fallback-state use; v1 G26's catchError clause and every catchError case would break.

decisions.chosen: The first error that reaches the sink unrecovered
decisions.why: Read as a whole, Spec §10.2 says an unhandled error ends the chain (principle 2) and gives catchError as the means to prevent it, so principle 5's 'first error' means the first one nothing on the path recovers. No Specification change is needed for that reading. This timestamp is an upper bound reconstructed from file birth times, because date -u was not run at the moment of the decision (see notes_for_orchestrator).

decisions.question: A stage that several sinks reach: which write chains does it belong to, and what does ending one of them cancel?

options.label: Every chain it feeds; cancel only what feeds no other live chain
options.consequence: Reference-counting semantics, as an Rx engine's shared pipeline has: the shared stage keeps running once per value for the live chain (G27), and an error raised in it ends every chain it reaches unrecovered while a chain whose catchError recovers it goes on.

options.label: Ending a chain cancels every stage of it, shared ones included
options.consequence: Stops chains that are still live, contradicting Spec §10.2 principle 5's 'the topology's other write chains keep running'; seeded as a defect it fails four G26 cases.

options.label: A shared stage belongs to the first sink's chain only
options.consequence: Ownership by declaration order: ending that chain stops a stage a live chain needs, or ending another leaves the shared stage's error ending chains it never reached; no Specification text supports it.

decisions.chosen: Every chain it feeds; cancel only what feeds no other live chain
decisions.why: Spec Appendix A.4 defines a chain as the whole pipeline one write connects to its topic, so overlapping pipelines are each a chain, and principle 5 keeps the other chains running. Cancelling by 'feeds no other live chain' is the only rule that satisfies both and keeps G27's stage sharing. This timestamp is an upper bound reconstructed from file birth times, because date -u was not run at the moment of the decision (see notes_for_orchestrator).
evidence: docs/auto-run/experiments/topology-dsl-write-chain/ T10 (defect: a shared stage cancelled with the chain that ended)

decisions.question: When does an ended chain's cancellation happen relative to the error that ends it?

options.label: At once, within the work that carried the error, without waiting for a cancel future
options.consequence: Deterministic under a VirtualScheduler with no real event-loop turn; the same rule ADR-003 item 3 and G22 already apply to switchMap and deactivation.

options.label: Before the scheduler is next quiescent
options.consequence: Looser for implementers; a value arriving in between could still run a function of the ended chain, so 'none of its functions runs again' would not hold.

options.label: After the sink subscription's cancel future completes
options.consequence: Chains on the SDK's root-zone future, which the virtual scheduler never sees (ADR-003 item 3); seeded as a defect it fails the inner-subscription case.

decisions.chosen: At once, within the work that carried the error, without waiting for a cancel future
decisions.why: ADR-003 item 3 forbids chaining on a cancel future anywhere in nidana, and the intake's prompt names it. Ending at once is what makes 'none of their functions runs again' exact. The stand-in meets it with synchronous cancellation of its hubs. This timestamp is an upper bound reconstructed from file birth times, because date -u was not run at the moment of the decision (see notes_for_orchestrator).
evidence: docs/auto-run/experiments/topology-dsl-write-chain/ T6, T8 (P1: no pending timer after the chain ends), T10 defect 1

decisions.question: The live suite's helper made every topology MODULE-scoped, and LiveTopologyHarness.start activates its topologies before start(), which Spec §7.2 'Scope timing' now rejects. How does the suite stay valid?

options.label: Topologies start activates are APPLICATION-scoped; post-start ones may be MODULE
options.consequence: Keeps the bootstrap path (connected at start()) under test and the harness interface unchanged, so bus-api's binding needs no change; three cases that activate only after the start use a MODULE topology.

options.label: Harness start starts first, then activates
options.consequence: Every topology connects at activate; the suite no longer exercises connection at start(); the harness text changes and bus-api's binding must change.

options.label: Leave the suite for H3 to adapt
options.consequence: Under a v0.15.1 bus the v1 suite passes 3 of 43 cases (T7); only this contract's step writes topology-dsl's fixtures, so H3 could not fix it.

decisions.chosen: Topologies start activates are APPLICATION-scoped; post-start ones may be MODULE
decisions.why: Spec §7.2 allows APPLICATION before start() and MODULE or PAGE only after it; this choice follows the rule while keeping both connection paths in the suite. Evidence: the barrier stand-in rejects the v1 suite's bootstrap MODULE activations and passes the v2 suite.
